strengths: Soundness: The expectation analysis has a coherent proof strategy based on the auxiliary sequence z_t, a monotone preconditioner, and bounds in terms of cumulative coordinatewise gradients. It usefully treats AMSGrad, modified RMSProp, and AdaGrad in one framework.
Significance: Convergence of adaptive optimizers is important, and improving the dimension dependence while pursuing single-run, high-probability guarantees would be valuable if fully established.
Presentation: The algorithms, assumptions, theorem constants, comparison table, and detailed proofs are provided, making the theoretical arguments unusually easy to audit.
Reproducibility and ethics: The main contribution is analytical and largely self-contained. The work involves no human subjects or sensitive data, and funding is disclosed.
weaknesses: Eligibility and originality are decisive: the supplied PDF states on every page that it was published in TMLR in February 2024, identifies all authors, and links its public OpenReview record. It is therefore neither new nor anonymous as an ICML 2026 main-track submission, independently precluding acceptance. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-bvgfcm66/call-280ca36c8d0945cc8cd259003de7f99d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Soundness: The central high-probability result is not proved as stated. From (A.17), moving the noise term to the left gives a coefficient α[(G∞+√ε)^−1−σ²α/ε]. Equation (A.20) instead writes α(G∞+√ε)^−1[1−σ²α/ε], dropping a factor of G∞+√ε. Thus the stated condition α≤ε/(2σ²) does not ensure the required positive descent coefficient; the displayed argument would require a stronger condition involving G∞+√ε or a different proof.

Soundness: Equation (B.15) uses ‖V̂₁^−1/2g₁‖∞≤1. For AMSGrad and modified RMSProp, v₁=(1−β₂)g₁², so the general bound is 1/√(1−β₂), not 1. Consequently, the explicit constants in the expectation theorem are also unsupported, although this issue may not change the asymptotic rate.

Significance: The favorable s<1/2 rate assumes ‖g₁:T,i‖₂≤G∞T^s for every coordinate. Persistent stochastic noise normally yields s=1/2, and the paper provides no distributional conditions ensuring a smaller exponent. Hence the worst-case result largely matches SGD rather than explaining an adaptive-method advantage.

Evidence and reproducibility: Appendix B.7 claims experiments with ResNet-18 and an LSTM but reports only one Penn Treebank table. It assumes G∞=1, does not explain how the coordinate index is aggregated when estimating s, and omits hyperparameters, seeds, uncertainty, and code. It therefore does not convincingly validate the key growth assumption.

Scope and presentation: The analyzed RMSProp includes AMSGrad's coordinatewise maximum and is not standard RMSProp, yet several broad claims simply say RMSProp. There is no substantive limitations discussion, and errors such as labeling the proof of Corollary 5.5 as Corollary 5.4 further reduce precision.

Originality assessment for 2026 is impossible from the literature review, which stops around 2020. Claims of first high-probability guarantees are both already published and unsupported relative to developments from 2021–2026.

strengths: The expectation analysis has a coherent technical core: the auxiliary momentum sequence and pathwise bounds on denominator-scaled gradients lead to a potentially useful dimension-sensitive rate.
The paper targets an important problem and attempts both expected and high-probability guarantees for AMSGrad, AdaGrad, and a max-corrected RMSProp variant.
Algorithms, output sampling, constants, proof sketches, and full appendix proofs are provided, making the theoretical claims comparatively easy to audit.
The work poses no evident human-subject, privacy, or broader safety concerns.
weaknesses: The main high-probability theorem is not proved as stated. After Eq. (A.17), the coefficient should be α[(G∞+√ε)^−1−ε^−1σ²α], equivalently α(G∞+√ε)^−1[1−(G∞+√ε)ε^−1σ²α]. The proof drops the factor G∞+√ε, so the stated condition α≤ε/(2σ²) need not leave a positive descent coefficient. A stronger condition depending on G∞ is required; consequently Theorem 5.2 and Corollaries 5.4–5.5 are unsupported as written.

There are additional proof defects. Eq. (B.15) implicitly uses ||V̂₁^−1/2g₁||∞≤1, whereas for AMSGrad it can approach (1−β₂)^−1/2. The generalized Lemma A.2 also simplifies a coefficient in a way that requires β₁′=β₁ despite presenting these parameters as independent. These issues may be repairable but invalidate the stated constants and generality.

The numbered assumptions omit the conditional unbiasedness and independence of fresh samples required in E[g_t|F_{t−1}]=∇f(x_t) and in the martingale argument. It is also unclear whether the random growth condition is required almost surely, in expectation, or only for the realized trajectory.

The claimed benefit for s<1/2 is weakly justified. Ordinary coordinate sparsity does not imply sub-square-root cumulative growth; a fixed sparse coordinate active at every iteration still has s=1/2, and persistent stochastic noise generally forces this worst case. The condition can therefore encode substantial gradient decay rather than sparsity alone.

Table 2 does not convincingly validate the growth assumption: it appears to estimate an asymptotic exponent from one horizon after setting G∞=1, without specifying coordinate aggregation, horizon, hyperparameters, seeds, or uncertainty. The text claims ResNet-18 and LSTM experiments, but only the LSTM result is reported and no code is supplied.

The abstract overstates scope by calling the results a general class analysis and referring to RMSProp, although the analyzed RMSProp includes AMSGrad's max correction and is not the standard algorithm. Dependence on strong bounded-gradient assumptions, horizon-dependent tuning, and constants that blow up as ε becomes small is not adequately discussed as a limitation.

For an ICML 2026 submission, the document's explicit status as already published in TMLR in February 2024 is independently disqualifying absent a permitted substantially extended version; it is also non-anonymous and publicly links the authors and prior OpenReview record. Moreover, the literature review largely stops in 2020, so originality relative to 2021–2026 work is not established.

strengths: Soundness: The AMSGrad analysis has a coherent descent-and-telescoping structure, explicit assumptions, and full supporting lemmas rather than relying only on proof sketches.

Significance: Nonconvex guarantees for adaptive optimizers are important, and controlling the adaptive terms through coordinatewise cumulative-gradient norms is a potentially useful analytical idea. High-probability guarantees would also be valuable if corrected.
Presentation and reproducibility: The algorithms, convergence measures, principal constants, and proofs are mostly stated explicitly; the comparison table makes the claimed advances easy to identify.
Research ethics: Apart from the prior-publication issue, this theoretical work and its public Penn Treebank experiment present no evident privacy, human-subject, or safety concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The AdaGrad corollaries are not supported by the proof. Lemma 6.4 bounds the AMSGrad accumulator by G_infinity squared, but Algorithm 3 uses a cumulative sum, so its accumulator can grow as T times G_infinity squared. Consequently, the uniform lower bound on the preconditioned gradient used in Theorems 4.3 and 5.2 does not transfer to AdaGrad; Corollaries 4.6 and 5.5 and their claimed dimension improvement therefore do not follow.

Soundness: The high-probability proof contains a consequential algebra error. After Eq. A.17, absorbing the noise term requires alpha to be smaller than epsilon divided by sigma squared times (G_infinity plus square-root epsilon), whereas the stated condition omits the latter factor. Theorem 5.2 is thus false under its stated step-size condition.

Soundness: Eq. B.15 assumes the first normalized gradient has infinity norm at most one. For AMSGrad/RMSProp it can instead approach 1/sqrt(1-beta_2), so the explicit theorem constants are also unjustified.

Originality and publication ethics: The reviewed PDF :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-g2228qid/call-86401bd1aab644ab9a4938136ef1de6e/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} explicitly identifies itself as arXiv:1808.05671v4 and as published in TMLR in February 2024. It therefore cannot constitute an original ICML 2026 main-track submission.

Significance and scope: The analyzed 'RMSProp' includes an AMSGrad-style running maximum and is not standard RMSProp, while Adam itself is not covered. Describing the work as applying to a general class of adaptive methods overstates its reach.

Evidence and reproducibility: The only empirical evidence is a small Penn Treebank table. The text also claims a ResNet-18 experiment that is not reported, and omits the definition/aggregation used to estimate s, hyperparameters, seeds, uncertainty, and code. It neither validates the convergence rates nor the dimension-dependence claim.

Limitations and presentation: There is no substantive discussion of the strong global bounded-gradient and pathwise growth assumptions, the questionable plausibility of s<1/2 under persistent stochastic noise, or horizon-dependent step-size selection. Several errors and inconsistencies—including duplicate Corollary 5.4 labels, 'RMSProf,' and the missing ResNet result—further impede reliable use of the results.

strengths: Soundness: The auxiliary momentum sequence and delayed preconditioner provide a useful framework for deriving expected stationary-point guarantees for AMSGrad, modified RMSProp, and AdaGrad.
Significance: Improving the dimension dependence and seeking high-probability guarantees for adaptive methods are meaningful theoretical objectives.
Presentation and reproducibility: The algorithms, assumptions, theorem constants, proof sketches, and full technical proofs are largely self-contained and clearly organized.
Ethics: The theoretical optimization work presents little direct societal or safety risk.
weaknesses: Originality is decisively inadequate for ICML 2026: the title page explicitly states that this work was published in TMLR in February 2024, identifies the authors, and links its OpenReview record. It is therefore neither a new archival contribution nor anonymous, and it raises a duplicate-publication concern.

The central high-probability result is unsupported as stated. When the noise penalty in (A.17) is absorbed on page 20, the correct coefficient is α/(G∞+√ε)·[1−σ²α(G∞+√ε)/ε], not α/(G∞+√ε)·[1−σ²α/ε]. The stated condition α≤ε/(2σ²) consequently does not establish Theorem 5.2 or its corollaries; this affects a headline contribution.

A second proof error occurs in (B.15): the claim that ‖V̂₁⁻¹ᐟ²g₁‖∞≤1 is false because V̂₁ contains (1−β₂)g₁²+ε. The ratio can approach 1/√(1−β₂), so the reported constants in the expectation and high-probability bounds are incorrect.

Significance is narrower than advertised: the analyzed “RMSProp” adds AMSGrad's coordinatewise maximum and is not standard RMSProp, while the improved rate relies on a pathwise cumulative-gradient growth condition, a horizon-dependent tuned step size, and averaged rather than last-iterate stationarity.

The empirical verification in Appendix B.7 is not reproducible or convincing. It mentions ResNet-18 but reports only one Penn Treebank table, does not define the estimator of s clearly, and omits hyperparameters, seeds, run counts, uncertainty, code, and coordinatewise evidence that the theorem's uniform growth condition holds.

Presentation has consequential ambiguities and errors, including inconsistent placement of ε in the optimizer denominator, no formal independent/unbiased-sampling assumption despite its use in the proofs, δ stated outside its meaningful range, and a duplicated/mislabeled Corollary 5.4 heading. There is also no substantive limitations discussion covering the strong bounded-gradient and growth assumptions or the gap from practical Adam training.

strengths: The technical approach is coherent and potentially reusable: the auxiliary sequence handles momentum, while Lemma 6.5/A.2 controls preconditioned gradients through coordinatewise gradient histories.

The paper states explicit expected-rate and high-probability results for AMSGrad, modified RMSProp, and AdaGrad. The data-dependent rate exposes how dimension and the gradient-growth parameter s enter the guarantee.

Algorithms, assumptions, constants, a proof sketch, full appendix proofs, and comparison tables make the theoretical argument relatively easy to audit. The manuscript is generally legible and well structured.
The topic is relevant, and the worst-case expected rate matches the cited stochastic nonconvex SGD rate while improving upon the dimension dependence of some cited adaptive-method bounds.
weaknesses: The decisive originality and publication-ethics issue is that the PDF explicitly says “Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (02/2024),” identifies the authors, gives an arXiv v4 date of June 2024, and links the completed OpenReview record. No new contribution relative to that publication is identified. This is therefore neither original nor anonymous as an ICML 2026 main-track submission and is ineligible absent an explicit venue exception. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-r1ohik5r/call-b642a8ed7a154d0f8d2e856f63481f31/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The high-probability theorem is not established as stated. From Eq. A.17, the useful coefficient is α/(G∞+√ε)−σ²α²/ε. Page 20 instead factors this as α(G∞+√ε)⁻¹(1−σ²α/ε), dropping a factor of G∞+√ε. Consequently, the stated condition α≤ε/(2σ²) is insufficient in general; the derivation would require a condition such as α≤ε/[2σ²(G∞+√ε)]. This affects Theorem 5.2 and Corollaries 5.4–5.5.

Lemma A.6 also uses the false inequality ‖V̂₁⁻¹ᐟ²g₁‖∞≤1 in Eq. B.15. For AMSGrad, v₁=(1−β₂)g₁², so a coordinate ratio equals |g₁|/√((1−β₂)g₁²+ε) and can approach 1/√(1−β₂)>1. Thus the displayed constants in the expected and high-probability AMSGrad bounds are unsupported, even if the asymptotic rate may be repairable.

The improved rate for s<1/2 rests on a path-dependent cumulative-gradient condition that is not justified for general stochastic optimization and is typically incompatible with persistent gradient noise. In the unconditional worst case s=1/2, the result only matches the standard SGD order. The manuscript does not establish optimality or a practically meaningful regime in which its finer rate applies.

The empirical verification of the growth condition is not reproducible. Section B.7 claims ResNet-18 and LSTM experiments but reports only one PennTreeBank LSTM table; it omits the ResNet result, hyperparameters, seeds, run counts, coordinate aggregation, a clear estimator for s, and code. Assuming G∞=1 is also left unexplained.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies: Eq. 1.1 uses √v̂+ε whereas the algorithms and proofs use √(v̂+ε); Theorem 4.3 quantifies its coordinatewise condition “for t=1,…,T” rather than for i=1,…,d; Appendix A.6 is mislabeled as another proof of Corollary 5.4; and the literature stops at 2020, making “first” claims inadequate for a 2026 submission.

There is no meaningful limitations discussion covering the globally bounded-gradient assumption, implicit independence of stochastic samples, the fact that the analyzed “RMSProp” includes an AMSGrad-style maximum and is not standard RMSProp, or the incomplete empirical support. The application itself has low societal risk, but the prior-publication issue is a material research-integrity concern.

strengths: Soundness: The auxiliary iterate and lagged-preconditioner analysis are useful ideas for handling momentum and adaptive stochastic denominators, while the coordinatewise cumulative-gradient lemma targets improved dimension dependence.
Significance: Convergence guarantees for AMSGrad, AdaGrad, and high-probability single-run behavior address an important optimization problem.
Presentation and reproducibility: Algorithms, assumptions, constants, proof sketches, and detailed appendices are provided, making most theoretical steps inspectable.
weaknesses: Originality and publication ethics are decisively problematic: the supplied manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-8kilef9k/call-6daf50046356446289ed46265cd28796/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} explicitly states that it was published in TMLR in February 2024 and displays the authors and OpenReview record. An unchanged archival publication is neither original to ICML 2026 nor double-blind and is ineligible for acceptance; this alone determines the strong-reject rating.
Soundness: Equation (B.15) uses ‖V̂₁⁻¹ᐟ²g₁‖∞≤1. Since v̂₁=(1−β₂)g₁², this ratio approaches 1/√(1−β₂), which exceeds one whenever β₂>0. Consequently, the stated finite constants are not proved.

Soundness: After (A.17), the high-probability proof incorrectly factors the noise term. From α‖∇f‖²/(G∞+√ε)−σ²α²‖∇f‖²/ε, absorption requires a step-size condition scaling as ε/[σ²(G∞+√ε)], not merely ε/σ². Thus the central high-probability theorem is unsupported as stated.

Evidence and significance: Improvements for s<1/2 require a pathwise, coordinatewise sublinear cumulative-gradient condition; persistent stochastic noise normally gives s=1/2. The lone LSTM table does not verify the uniform condition, arbitrarily sets G∞=1, omits how coordinates are aggregated, and provides no runs or uncertainty. The text also promises ResNet-18 results that are absent.

Scope is narrower than the framing suggests: the analyzed “RMSProp” adds a monotone maximum and is therefore not ordinary RMSProp, Adam is not covered, and the guarantees require bounded stochastic gradients, horizon-dependent tuning, and potentially unfavorable ε and momentum constants.

Presentation and reproducibility weaknesses include missing experimental hyperparameters, horizon, code, and repeated trials; theorem-index and notation errors; an inconsistent RMSProp constant in Corollary 5.4; and no substantive limitations discussion. The literature review also stops around 2020, so novelty claims are not situated against work available by 2026.

Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Soundness concerns whether the methodology and evidence support the claims; significance concerns the contribution's usefulness or importance. Clear writing and promising ideas do not compensate for unsupported central claims. A modest or specialized contribution can still be useful, and originality may arise through new understanding rather than an entirely new method.

Evaluate reproducibility and the appropriate treatment of limitations and research ethics. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses using evidence from the manuscript. Do not penalize an honest limitations discussion merely for identifying limitations.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject

strengths: Soundness: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-fylp0kca/call-6b4e1cc0755e4907b8bef96f831720e6/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} develops a coherent auxiliary-sequence analysis that handles momentum while lagging the adaptive preconditioner, and it supplies detailed proofs rather than only proof sketches.

Significance: The intended results—improving the worst-case dimension dependence to O(sqrt(d/T)+d/T) and deriving high-probability guarantees for several adaptive methods—address useful questions in nonconvex optimization.
Originality: At the work's original time, the data-dependent rate and high-probability analysis represented potentially meaningful theoretical advances over the cited AMSGrad and AdaGrad bounds.
Presentation: The algorithms, assumptions, output criterion, comparison table, theorem constants, and proof structure are generally easy to locate and follow.
Ethics: The technical subject and standard Penn Treebank experiment present no evident human-subject, privacy, or deployment risks.
weaknesses: Originality and publication ethics are decisive: the supplied manuscript explicitly states that it was published in TMLR in February 2024 and identifies itself as arXiv:1808.05671v4, with authors and an OpenReview link. It is therefore neither an original nor anonymous ICML 2026 submission and cannot be accepted in the main track.

Soundness: The central high-probability result has an algebraic gap. Equation (A.17) contributes epsilon^{-1} sigma^2 alpha^2 times the sum of squared gradient norms, while the descent term is only lower-bounded by alpha/(G_infinity+sqrt(epsilon)) times that sum. The coefficient should consequently contain 1-(G_infinity+sqrt(epsilon))sigma^2 alpha/epsilon, but page 20 omits the G_infinity+sqrt(epsilon) factor. Thus Theorem 5.2's condition alpha <= epsilon/(2 sigma^2) is insufficient in general; a condition such as alpha <= epsilon/[2 sigma^2(G_infinity+sqrt(epsilon))] would be needed for this argument. Corollaries 5.4 and 5.5 inherit the issue.

Soundness: Equation (B.15) uses ||Vhat_1^{-1/2}g_1||_infinity <= 1, which does not follow from the algorithm: since v_1=(1-beta_2)g_1^2, the ratio can approach 1/sqrt(1-beta_2). This invalidates the stated constants even if the asymptotic rate may be repairable.

Significance: The favorable s<1/2 rate assumes every coordinate's realized cumulative stochastic-gradient norm is bounded by G_infinity T^s. Ordinary persistent stochastic noise generally forces s=1/2, and per-iteration coordinate sparsity alone does not imply a smaller exponent. strengths: Soundness (partial): The AMSGrad analysis uses a sensible auxiliary sequence and a lagged preconditioner to recover conditional unbiasedness. Assumptions, constants, supporting lemmas, and full proofs are provided.

Significance: Dimension-sensitive stationarity bounds and high-probability guarantees for adaptive optimizers are important targets. The claimed sparsity-dependent refinement would be useful if correct.
Presentation: The algorithms, comparison table, proof sketches, and appendix make the intended argument relatively easy to audit, and the PDF is visually legible.
Reproducibility (theory): The update rules and most theorem parameters are explicit enough to permit independent checking.
weaknesses: Soundness: The AdaGrad results are invalidly derived. Lemma A.1 bounds the AMSGrad exponential accumulator by G_infinity^2, but Algorithm 3 accumulates squared gradients, so its accumulator can grow as t G_infinity^2. Nevertheless, Corollaries 4.6 and 5.5 reuse the resulting lower bound on the preconditioner unchanged. A one-dimensional example such as f(x)=log(cosh(x)) with alpha=T^(-1/2) already contradicts the claimed vanishing bound: AdaGrad moves only O(1) distance while the stated right-hand side tends to zero.

Soundness: The high-probability proof contains a separate algebraic error after Eq. A.17. The coefficient is alpha/(G_infinity+sqrt(epsilon)) minus sigma^2 alpha^2/epsilon, but page 20 factors it as alpha/(G_infinity+sqrt(epsilon)) times (1-sigma^2 alpha/epsilon). The stated condition alpha <= epsilon/(2 sigma^2) is therefore insufficient; the displayed argument requires at least alpha <= epsilon/[2 sigma^2(G_infinity+sqrt(epsilon))]. Theorem 5.2 and its corollaries are unsupported as written.

Significance: The analyzed “RMSProp” adds AMSGrad's coordinatewise maximum and is not standard RMSProp. The worst-case result only matches SGD, while no lower bound, tightness analysis, or convincing experiment demonstrates practical benefit.

Significance: The data-dependent rate O(sqrt(d)/T^(3/4-s/2)+d/T) gives an informative interpolation through the cumulative-gradient parameter s and improves the dimension dependence of the cited earlier analyses.
Presentation and reproducibility: The algorithms, main theorem, comparison table, proof sketch, and full derivations are organized clearly, making the theoretical claims relatively easy to inspect.
Research ethics: As optimization theory using standard benchmark data, the work presents no apparent human-subject, privacy, or direct societal-risk concerns.
weaknesses: Originality and publication ethics are decisively disqualifying: the reviewed PDF :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-8lwpqkws/call-cf11401fb41b4aa89f0da313ef25f087/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} explicitly identifies itself as arXiv:1808.05671v4 and as published in TMLR in February 2024, provides an existing OpenReview link, and reveals all authors. Soundness: The proof of the central high-probability result appears algebraically invalid as written. After (A.17), moving the noise term and factoring should produce 1-(G_infinity+sqrt(epsilon))sigma^2 alpha/epsilon, but page 20 uses 1-sigma^2 alpha/epsilon. Consequently, the stated condition alpha<=epsilon/(2 sigma^2) does not justify Theorem 5.2 without an additional restriction or a corrected argument.

Significance and limitations: There is no evaluation of convergence rates or bound tightness. The analyzed 'RMSProp' includes AMSGrad's max correction and is not standard RMSProp, Adam itself is not covered, the optimized step size requires advance knowledge of T and s, and constants deteriorate sharply with small epsilon. These limitations are not adequately discussed.

Presentation and formal precision: The theory does not explicitly state the conditional independence/unbiased-oracle assumption used after conditioning on the history or require a finite lower bound on f. Additional issues include δ being allowed outside (0,1), theorem indices saying 'for t' where 'for i' is intended, incorrect cross-references, duplicated Corollary 5.4 appendix headings, and a related-work record ending in 2020 that cannot substantiate 2026 novelty claims.

weaknesses: Originality/ethics/eligibility are decisively deficient: the manuscript explicitly states that it was published in TMLR in February 2024, identifies all authors, and links its public OpenReview record. It is therefore neither anonymous nor an original unpublished ICML 2026 main-track submission; prior archival publication alone precludes acceptance.

The headline high-probability theorem is not proved under its stated step-size condition. From (A.17), moving the variance term gives coefficient alpha/(G_infinity+sqrt(epsilon)) - sigma^2 alpha^2/epsilon = alpha/(G_infinity+sqrt(epsilon))[1-(G_infinity+sqrt(epsilon))sigma^2 alpha/epsilon]. strengths: Soundness: The expectation analysis has a coherent proof strategy: a lagged preconditioner and auxiliary sequence handle the dependence introduced by momentum, and the manuscript supplies explicit assumptions, constants, and detailed appendix proofs.

Significance: The data-dependent rate in terms of cumulative-gradient growth and the attempted high-probability extensions for AMSGrad, modified RMSProp, and AdaGrad address a useful theoretical question.
Presentation: Algorithms, principal results, and comparison tables are organized clearly, with proof sketches in the main text and technical details in the appendix.
Reproducibility of the theoretical component is relatively strong because the update rules, parameter restrictions, lemmas, and derivations are mostly stated explicitly.
weaknesses: Originality and eligibility are decisive: the PDF :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-n8nu6sdt/call-c1b523a75d1a4ff4a5ef73080c3ae40a/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} explicitly identifies itself as published in TMLR in February 2024, lists named authors, institutions and emails, and links its OpenReview record. It therefore provides no original ICML 2026 contribution and raises a fundamental duplicate-submission/provenance concern, including conflict with the stated DeepSeek-V4-Pro authorship.

Soundness: The high-probability proof contains an algebraic error between (A.17) and page 20. Absorbing the noise term should produce the factor 1−σ²α(G∞+√ε)/ε, whereas the manuscript uses 1−σ²α/ε. Consequently, α≤ε/(2σ²) is insufficient; Theorem 5.2 and Corollaries 5.4–5.5 are not established as stated.

Soundness: Equation (B.15) assumes ‖V̂₁⁻¹ᐟ²g₁‖∞≤1. For AMSGrad and modified RMSProp, v₁=(1−β₂)g₁², so this quantity can approach (1−β₂)⁻¹ᐟ². The advertised finite-sample constants therefore do not follow from the proof.

The practical reach is limited. The RMSProp result concerns a nonstandard version augmented with AMSGrad's running maximum; the worst-case rate merely matches SGD; and improvement requires a pathwise, coordinatewise condition ‖g₁:T,i‖₂≤G∞Tˢ together with tuning that depends on s.

Empirical support and reproducibility are inadequate. Table 2 gives one scalar s for an LSTM/Penn Treebank experiment without seeds, horizon, hyperparameters, fitting procedure, coordinate aggregation, or code. It does not verify the theorem's uniform per-coordinate condition, and the text mentions a ResNet-18 experiment that is not reported.

The manuscript does not adequately discuss limitations such as globally bounded stochastic gradients, sub-Gaussian noise, dependence of dimension comparisons on norm conventions, and the gap between stationary-point guarantees and practical deep-learning performance. It also uses literature ending around 2020, inconsistent optimizer definitions for ε, duplicated/mislabeled appendix headings, and a non-anonymous previously published format.

strengths: Soundness: The paper develops a coherent framework for AMSGrad, max-corrected RMSProp, and AdaGrad, with explicit assumptions, proof sketches, and detailed proofs.

Significance: If correct, the data-dependent expected rate and improved dimension dependence would be useful theoretical results; the auxiliary-sequence analysis and gradient-history bound are technically interesting.
Presentation/reproducibility: Algorithms, constants, and comparisons with prior bounds are mostly stated explicitly, and the mathematical appendix is substantial.
Research ethics: This is theoretical optimization research with no evident human-subject, privacy, safety, or other material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Originality/eligibility: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-u6qnypam/call-bb96afb08882490396378da1a821065a/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} explicitly says it was published in TMLR in February 2024 and supplies an arXiv version, authors, and an OpenReview page. It therefore is neither new nor anonymous as an ICML 2026 main-track submission, independently precluding acceptance.

Soundness: The central high-probability proof contains an invalid algebraic step. After (A.17), moving the variance term gives coefficient α/(G∞+√ε)−σ²α²/ε, but page 20 replaces this by α(G∞+√ε)^{-1}(1−σ²α/ε). Consequently, the claimed condition α≤ε/(2σ²) does not establish Theorem 5.2; a dependence on G∞+√ε is missing. This undermines one of the headline contributions and all derived high-probability corollaries as stated.

Soundness: In (B.15), the proof assumes ||V̂_1^{-1/2}g_1||∞≤1. For AMSGrad/RMSProp, v_1=(1−β₂)g_1², so the available bound is instead 1/√(1−β₂). Thus the advertised finite constants for the expected bounds are also not justified as written.

Significance: Improvements beyond the worst case rely on the pathwise condition ||g_{1:T,i}||₂≤G∞T^s with s<1/2. For raw stochastic gradients with persistent nonzero noise, this quantity ordinarily scales as √T, giving only s=1/2. The assumption is not given a probabilistically precise formulation, substantially limiting the claimed practical interpretation.

Scope is overstated: the analyzed “RMSProp” includes a running maximum and is not standard RMSProp. Moreover, equation (1.1) uses √v̂+ε while the algorithms and proofs use √(v̂+ε), leaving the exact analyzed implementation inconsistent.

Reproducibility/evidence: The sole empirical evidence is Table 2 for one LSTM/Penn Treebank setting. Although the text also claims a ResNet-18 experiment, none is reported. Training details, horizons, seeds, coordinate aggregation, the procedure for estimating s, and code are absent, so the key growth-condition claim cannot be reproduced.

Limitations/presentation: There is no meaningful limitations discussion covering the global bounded-gradient assumption, horizon-dependent step-size tuning, restrictive growth condition, or modified algorithms. Several theorem quantifiers and corollary labels are also erroneous. These issues make the manuscript difficult to rely upon even apart from its prior publication.

The auxiliary iterate and predictable preconditioner provide a coherent basis for the expected-rate analysis.
Significance: Improving the cited dimension dependence and pursuing high-probability guarantees for adaptive nonconvex optimization are useful theoretical goals.
Presentation and reproducibility: The core algorithms and theorem dependencies are easy to locate, and most of the theoretical derivation is sufficiently detailed to audit.
Ethics: Beyond the publication-status issue, this optimization-theory work presents no evident human-subject, privacy, or safety concerns.
weaknesses: Originality and eligibility are decisive: every page identifies the work as published in TMLR in February 2024, while the title page supplies authors, emails, and its OpenReview record. As submitted to the ICML 2026 main track, it is neither original nor anonymous and would be ineligible irrespective of technical merit.

Soundness: The central high-probability result is not proved under its stated step-size condition. After (A.17), moving the variance term gives α[(G∞+√ε)^−1−σ²α/ε], but page 20 incorrectly rewrites this as α(G∞+√ε)^−1(1−σ²α/ε). The claimed α≤ε/(2σ²) is therefore insufficient; the displayed argument requires an additional factor involving G∞+√ε. Theorem 5.2 and both high-probability corollaries consequently do not follow as stated.

Soundness: Equation (B.15) assumes ||V̂₁^−1/2g₁||∞≤1. For AMSGrad/RMSProp, however, v̂₁=(1−β₂)g₁², so this quantity can approach 1/√(1−β₂). Thus Lemma A.6 and the explicit constants in the expectation guarantees are also unsupported, although the asymptotic rate may be repairable.

Evidence and reproducibility: The favorable s<1/2 rates require a pathwise growth condition on cumulative stochastic-gradient energy whose probabilistic meaning is not specified. Appendix B.7 gives only one unexplained Penn Treebank table—without code, seeds, hyperparameters, coordinate aggregation, or estimation procedure—and mentions a ResNet-18 experiment that is not reported.

Significance and limitations: The paper analyzes a max-corrected RMSProp rather than standard RMSProp, does not analyze Adam, requires bounded gradients and horizon-dependent tuning using d and s, and does not discuss these restrictions adequately. Dimension comparisons also mix ℓ∞-, ℓ2-, and sub-Gaussian assumptions.

Presentation: The bibliography ends around 2020 and cannot support 2026 novelty claims. Repeated numbering errors, inconsistent constants, and garbled experimental prose further hinder verification. Even disregarding the prior-publication violation, the theorem-level gaps warrant rejection.

strengths: The expected-convergence analysis is technically motivated and largely self-contained: it clearly defines AMSGrad, a max-corrected RMSProp variant, and AdaGrad, then uses an auxiliary momentum sequence and coordinate-wise cumulative-gradient bounds to derive data-dependent rates.
The topic is significant. Dimension-sensitive and high-probability guarantees for adaptive methods in nonconvex stochastic optimization would be useful if established correctly.
The main assumptions, theorem constants, algorithms, comparison table, and extensive appendices make the theoretical argument reasonably auditable. The PDF is also visually clear and well organized.
The growth-rate formulation can yield sharper guarantees when the coordinate-wise cumulative gradients genuinely grow slower than the worst-case square-root rate.
weaknesses: Decisive originality/eligibility failure: the submitted PDF :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-mtelwwq6/call-35c65b01a0c54bc687394dddff7ec4a9/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} explicitly states that this work was published in TMLR in February 2024 and links its completed OpenReview record. It also exposes authors, affiliations, and emails. Thus it is neither an original nor anonymous ICML 2026 main-track submission, which alone necessitates rejection.

The central high-probability result is not proved as stated. From Eq. (A.17), the martingale penalty is sigma^2 alpha^2/epsilon times the summed squared gradients, whereas the descent term is only lower-bounded by alpha/(G_infinity+sqrt(epsilon)) times that sum. The absorbable factor should therefore contain 1-(G_infinity+sqrt(epsilon))sigma^2 alpha/epsilon, but page 20 writes 1-sigma^2 alpha/epsilon. Consequently, the stated condition alpha <= epsilon/(2 sigma^2) is insufficient without an unstated normalization; Theorem 5.2 and its corollaries require correction.

Another proof error occurs in Eq. (B.15): the claim that the infinity norm of V_1^{-1/2}g_1 is at most one is false for AMSGrad/RMSProp because v_1=(1-beta_2)g_1^2. The ratio can approach 1/sqrt(1-beta_2), so the advertised constants are invalid. The generalized Lemma A.2 also simplifies a coefficient using beta'_1 as though beta'_1=beta_1, despite being stated for independent parameters.

The practical interpretation of s<1/2 is weakly supported. Coordinate sparsity alone does not imply sub-square-root temporal cumulative-gradient growth, especially under persistent stochastic noise. The assumption must hold pathwise for every coordinate, and the horizon-dependent stepsize uses the unknown s.

Claims about RMSProp are overstated: the analyzed algorithm includes AMSGrad's coordinate-wise maximum and is therefore not standard RMSProp, although the abstract and conclusion sometimes omit this qualification.

The sole empirical validation is not reproducible. Appendix B.7 does not define how s is aggregated or fitted, provides no hyperparameters, preprocessing, seeds, uncertainty, or code, and reports only the LSTM/Penn Treebank table despite claiming ResNet-18 experiments.

The related-work coverage ends around 2020 and cannot substantiate novelty claims for ICML 2026. There is also no substantive limitations discussion covering the bounded-gradient assumption, modified-RMSProp scope, pathwise growth condition, or horizon-tuned stepsize. Direct societal risk is low, but the undisclosed-to-the-venue prior-publication and anonymity issues are material research-integrity concerns.

strengths: The paper addresses an important optimization question and gives explicit algorithms and convergence statements for AMSGrad, AdaGrad, and a max-corrected RMSProp variant.

The auxiliary momentum sequence and predictable preconditioner provide a useful proof strategy, while the cumulative-coordinate-gradient lemma offers potentially improved dimension dependence under its stated growth condition.

Presentation is generally well organized, with a comparison table, proof sketches, and full appendices. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-lk0i1ooj/call-ba4b8d0364464c5b8a5a992fc51564a5/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The research poses no apparent human-subject, privacy, or harmful-use concerns.
weaknesses: Originality and eligibility are decisive problems: the first page explicitly states that this work was published in TMLR in February 2024, identifies the authors, and links its arXiv and OpenReview records. Without a materially new contribution, it is neither original nor anonymous for an ICML 2026 submission and raises a fundamental prior-publication concern.

The central high-probability theorem is not proved as stated. Moving the variance term in (6.14)/(A.17) yields the coefficient α[(G∞+√ε)^(-1)−σ²α/ε], whereas page 20 uses α(G∞+√ε)^(-1)(1−σ²α/ε). The missing factor G∞+√ε means the claimed condition α≤ε/(2σ²) is insufficient; Theorem 5.2 and its corollaries require correction.

Equation (B.15) incorrectly assumes ||V̂₁^(-1/2)g₁||∞≤1. For AMSGrad, v₁=(1−β₂)g₁², so this quantity can approach 1/√(1−β₂). Consequently, even the stated constants in the expectation result are unsupported.

The faster rates rely on the random, trajectory-level condition ||g₁:T,i||₂≤G∞T^s, but the paper does not specify whether it must hold almost surely or on an event. With persistent stochastic noise, s<1/2 is generally implausible; at s=1/2 the result only matches SGD's iteration rate.

Significance is limited by analyzing corrected RMSProp rather than standard RMSProp, excluding Adam, and comparing dimension dependence under different norm/noise assumptions. Constants also deteriorate as ε becomes small.

The empirical support is not reproducible: Appendix B.7 provides one Penn Treebank table without hyperparameters, seeds, uncertainty, coordinate aggregation, or exponent-fitting details, and mentions ResNet-18 experiments without reporting them. No code is provided.

The literature ends around 2020 and is inadequate for a 2026 originality claim. The manuscript also lacks a substantive limitations discussion and contains numerous inconsistencies, including duplicate “Proof of Corollary 5.4” headings, incorrect cross-references, and typographical errors.

strengths: Soundness: The expected-convergence analysis has a coherent structure: the auxiliary momentum sequence, predictable preconditioner, and coordinatewise energy bound lead to explicit AMSGrad, modified-RMSProp, and AdaGrad rates, with detailed proofs rather than unsupported assertions.
Significance: Improving the dimension dependence of nonconvex adaptive-method guarantees and pursuing single-run, high-probability guarantees address useful optimization-theory questions.

Presentation: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-lcb7nm3n/call-9faf6da6d4b54ff082b9cecc07c4c857/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} clearly states algorithms, assumptions, theorem constants, comparisons, proof sketches, and full appendices; the rendered equations and tables are legible.

Originality relative to the cited literature: The combination of improved dimension dependence and high-probability analysis for AMSGrad was a meaningful conceptual contribution when compared with the 2018–2020 results discussed in the paper.
Ethics: The work is mathematical optimization research using a standard public benchmark, with no evident direct societal or human-subject risks.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: The high-probability proof contains an algebraic error between (A.17) and page 20. The descent term contributes α/(G∞+√ε) times the summed squared gradients, whereas the noise term contributes ε⁻¹σ²α² times that sum. Their difference is α[(G∞+√ε)⁻¹−ε⁻¹σ²α], not α(G∞+√ε)⁻¹(1−ε⁻¹σ²α) as written. Consequently, α≤ε/(2σ²) does not justify Theorem 5.2; a condition involving an additional G∞+√ε factor or a revised concentration argument and constants is needed. This affects Theorem 5.2 and Corollaries 5.4–5.5, which constitute a central claimed contribution.

Soundness: Equation (B.15) uses ‖V̂₁⁻¹ᐟ²g₁‖∞≤1. Since v̂₁=(1−β₂)g₁², this ratio can approach 1/√(1−β₂), so the stated inequality and resulting constants in the expectation theorem are not valid for general β₂. The generalized Lemma A.2 also drops the factor (1−β₁′)²/(1−β₁) without imposing the condition needed to replace it by 1−β₁′.

Evidence and significance: The favorable s<1/2 rate assumes a pathwise, per-coordinate cumulative-gradient condition. Ordinary gradient sparsity does not by itself imply a sub-square-root temporal growth exponent. Appendix B.7 supplies only a finite-horizon scalar estimate and therefore does not verify the asymptotic condition required by the theorem.

Reproducibility: Appendix B.7 claims ResNet-18 and LSTM experiments but reports only the LSTM table. It does not define how s is aggregated across coordinates, nor provide training configuration, horizon, seeds, variability, or code, so the empirical claim cannot be reproduced reliably.

Scope: The analyzed “RMSProp” adds the AMSGrad maximum operation and is not standard RMSProp; the abstract and conclusion sometimes omit this qualification. Despite describing a general class, the results do not cover Adam, the practically central method.

Presentation and limitations: There is no substantive limitations discussion of the globally bounded stochastic-gradient assumption, horizon- and dimension-dependent step-size choice, restrictive growth condition, or absence of optimizer-performance experiments. There are also numerous cross-reference and notation errors, including calling the Theorem 5.2 sketch “Theorem 4.3,” writing log(2/ε) where δ is intended, and labeling the proof of Corollary 5.5 as Corollary 5.4.

Originality and publication ethics for this venue are fatal: the file explicitly says it was published in TMLR in February 2024, includes an arXiv identifier, author identities, and its OpenReview page. It is therefore neither original nor anonymous as an ICML 2026 main-track submission. Moreover, the related-work discussion stops at 2020 and cannot establish novelty against the 2021–2026 literature. Even setting eligibility aside, the unresolved errors in the central high-probability result prevent acceptance.

strengths: Soundness: The paper gives a coherent proof strategy, using the auxiliary sequence z_t to separate momentum and adaptive-preconditioner effects, and includes detailed proofs rather than only informal arguments.
Significance: Dimension-sensitive stationarity rates and single-run, high-probability guarantees for adaptive optimizers are worthwhile theoretical targets.

Presentation: The algorithms, assumptions, principal theorems, comparison table, and proof sketches are organized clearly, and the distinction between expectation and high-probability results is easy to follow.

Reproducibility and ethics: The theoretical algorithms and most derivations are specified in the appendix. The optimization problem itself raises no evident human-subject, privacy, or safety concerns.
weaknesses: Originality and eligibility are decisive: the front matter explicitly identifies this as an already published Transactions on Machine Learning Research paper from February 2024, provides an arXiv identifier and OpenReview link, and reveals all authors and affiliations. An identical previously published, non-anonymous work is not eligible as an original ICML 2026 main-track submission, regardless of how openly this is disclosed.

Soundness: The central high-probability argument contains an algebraic error after Eq. (A.17). The available terms give a coefficient α/(G∞+√ε)−σ²α²/ε on the summed gradient norm, but the proof factors this as α/(G∞+√ε)(1−σ²α/ε), omitting G∞+√ε from the second factor. Consequently, the stated condition α≤ε/(2σ²) does not ensure a positive descent coefficient for the theorem's unrestricted G∞ and ε. Theorem 5.2 and its high-probability corollaries are therefore unsupported as stated.

Soundness: Eq. (B.15) assumes ||V̂_1^−1/2 g_1||∞≤1. For AMSGrad, a coordinate equals |g|/sqrt((1−β2)g²+ε), which can exceed one. Thus the claimed dαG∞ bound and the explicit theorem constants are not valid without an additional factor or assumption.

The improvement for s<1/2 rests on a strong trajectory-wise condition, ||g_{1:T,i}||₂≤G∞T^s for every coordinate. Temporal or coordinate sparsity alone does not establish this under persistent stochastic noise, and the algorithm must select a step size using the unknown s and horizon T. The unconditional result is only the s=1/2 worst case.

The scope is overstated: the analyzed “RMSProp” includes AMSGrad's coordinatewise maximum and is therefore not standard RMSProp. The analyzed algorithms also omit bias correction and use sqrt(v+ε), whereas the introductory update uses sqrt(v)+ε.

Empirical reproducibility is inadequate. Appendix B.7 provides only one LSTM/Penn Treebank table despite mentioning ResNet-18, and omits the training horizon, optimizer settings, seeds, coordinate aggregation used to estimate s, uncertainty, and code. Assuming G∞=1 is not justified, although its value directly affects the claimed growth exponent.

Presentation has numerous consequential inconsistencies, including an ill-indexed condition in Theorem 4.3, “RMSProf,” two appendices labeled as proofs of Corollary 5.4 instead of including Corollary 5.5, and log(2/ε) where log(2/δ) is intended.

The paper has no substantive limitations discussion and its literature review ends around 2020. It therefore neither explains the practical restrictions of its global bounded-gradient and pathwise-growth assumptions nor establishes significance or novelty relative to work available by ICML 2026.

strengths: The paper addresses an important optimization question and gives a unified treatment of AMSGrad, modified RMSProp, and AdaGrad for smooth stochastic nonconvex objectives.

The coordinatewise cumulative-gradient analysis yields an informative data-dependent bound and, in the worst case, a potentially useful improvement in explicit dimension dependence over the cited analyses.

The main proof strategy is explained through an auxiliary momentum sequence, and the manuscript includes algorithms, comparison tables, proof sketches, and full appendices, making the theoretical argument relatively easy to audit.
The work presents no evident human-subject, privacy, or deployment-related ethical risks, and funding is disclosed.
weaknesses: Originality is decisively inadequate for ICML 2026: the title page explicitly identifies this manuscript as published in TMLR in February 2024, provides its OpenReview page, and shows arXiv:1808.05671v4. It is also non-anonymized. Prior publication alone precludes acceptance as a new main-track contribution.

The central high-probability theorem is not established as stated. After (A.17), absorbing ε⁻¹σ²α²∑‖∇f(x_t)‖² into the lower bound α(G∞+√ε)⁻¹∑‖∇f(x_t)‖² produces the factor 1−σ²α(G∞+√ε)/ε. The proof instead uses 1−σ²α/ε. Consequently, α≤ε/(2σ²) is insufficient; a condition such as α≤ε/[2σ²(G∞+√ε)] is required.

The expectation proof also contains a false initial-step bound in (B.15). For AMSGrad, v̂₁=(1−β₂)g₁², so ‖V̂₁⁻¹ᐟ²g₁‖∞ can approach 1/√(1−β₂), not 1. This missing factor propagates into the stated constants for AMSGrad and modified RMSProp.

The claimed advantage for s<1/2 rests on a strong trajectory-dependent assumption ‖g_{1:T,i}‖₂≤G∞Tˢ. Persistent stochastic noise generally gives s=1/2 even when individual gradients are sparse, so the manuscript's assertion that sparsity implies s<1/2 is unsupported. The tuned step size also depends on the unknown s and horizon T.

Empirical evidence is inadequate and irreproducible. The appendix reports one Penn Treebank/LSTM table without seeds, uncertainty, hyperparameters, gradient aggregation details, training horizon, or code; it claims experiments with ResNet-18 but presents no corresponding result. It does not test the advertised convergence or dimension scaling.

The algorithm is ambiguously specified: (1.1) uses √v̂+ε whereas the algorithms and proofs use √(v̂+ε), and the method called RMSProp includes an AMSGrad-style running maximum rather than being standard RMSProp.

Presentation is generally readable but contains substantive copy and consistency problems, including incorrect theorem references, duplicate labeling of Corollary 5.4, and RMSProf. The related work stops around 2020, and there is no proper limitations discussion covering bounded gradients, the growth condition, hidden parameter dependence, or the mismatch between the Gaussian example and the simultaneously imposed almost-sure bounded-gradient assumption.

strengths: The auxiliary-sequence analysis and delayed preconditioner provide a coherent route to expectation bounds for AMSGrad, modified RMSProp, and AdaGrad. Algorithms, assumptions, and proofs are largely self-contained. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-ng9mjz98/call-c9b2809ff4534addb5bbaf862ca89221/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The improved worst-case dimension dependence, O(sqrt(d/T)+d/T), and the attempted high-probability extension address meaningful theoretical questions about widely used adaptive optimizers.
The comparison table, proof sketches, explicit constants, and complete appendix make the intended contribution relatively easy to audit.
The work is theoretical and uses a standard public language-modeling dataset; it presents no evident human-subject, privacy, or broader societal-risk concerns.
weaknesses: The central high-probability proof has a concrete algebraic gap. After (A.17), the descent coefficient should be alpha/(G_inf+sqrt(epsilon)) - sigma^2 alpha^2/epsilon, equivalently alpha/(G_inf+sqrt(epsilon))[1-(G_inf+sqrt(epsilon))sigma^2 alpha/epsilon]. Page 20 drops the G_inf+sqrt(epsilon) factor. Consequently, the stated condition alpha <= epsilon/(2 sigma^2) does not justify Theorem 5.2 or its corollaries for general G_inf.

A second false bound occurs in (B.15): ||Vhat_1^{-1/2}g_1||_inf <= 1 need not hold because v_1=(1-beta_2)g_1^2; the ratio can approach 1/sqrt(1-beta_2). Thus, even the expectation theorem's displayed constants are unsupported. The generalized Lemma A.2 also silently needs beta'_1 >= beta_1 and gamma<1, rather than its stated conditions.

The practical scope is overstated. The analyzed “RMSProp” includes an AMSGrad-style running maximum and is not standard RMSProp. Moreover, the favorable s<1/2 rate assumes a pathwise, coordinatewise cumulative-gradient condition that ordinary gradient sparsity does not itself imply.

The lone empirical table cannot validate that asymptotic condition: the estimator for s, coordinate aggregation, horizon, hyperparameters, seeds, and uncertainty are omitted; ResNet-18 is mentioned but no corresponding result is reported. No code or adequate replication details are supplied.

The paper lacks a candid limitations discussion, contains numerous notation and cross-reference errors, and surveys literature only through 2020, leaving its “first” and originality claims inadequately supported for ICML 2026.

The supplied PDF explicitly states that it was published in TMLR in February 2024 and reveals authors, affiliations, acknowledgments, an arXiv identifier, and an OpenReview link. If treated literally as an ICML 2026 submission, prior-publication eligibility and anonymization require immediate program-chair review. Even setting that procedural issue aside, the theorem gaps warrant revision before acceptance.
